title: Havdalah at home
hook: the candle, the spices, the wine, with everyone in the house
tomorrow: after several Shabbatot, what do you keep, and what do you drop?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the portion: twice to hear it, once to understand it, in step with everyone reading it that week. Morning of the portion. Now the day is ending, and the house gathers to say goodbye to it.
screen: `MORNING OF THE PORTION.` → `THE DAY IS ENDING.`

segments.voice: Every family has one argument that never ends: is it pronounced this way or that, does the milk go in first. The schools of Shammai and Hillel had one over a single word in Havdalah, the short ceremony that closes Shabbat with a candle, sweet spices and a cup of wine. The blessing over the fire. One school said: who created the light of the fire. The other said: who creates the lights of the fire. One light, or many? Both sides deserve a hearing.
screen: `ONE ARGUMENT THAT NEVER ENDS.` → `THE BLESSING OVER THE FIRE.` → `ONE LIGHT, OR MANY?`

segments.voice: The Mishnah records both wordings, and the Talmud explains the disagreement: the House of Shammai held that there is one light in fire; the House of Hillel, that there are many lights in it. Shammai's best case: fire is one thing, from one source. Name it as one, and you keep whole what God made whole. Hillel's best case: look closely at a flame and it isn't one color; the blessing should name what's actually in front of your eyes. The law follows Hillel, and so a Havdalah candle is often braided, several wicks burning as one flame, many lights you can see. The Mishnah adds a small rule with a big picture inside it: don't bless the light until you've had some use of it. So people hold up their hands and look at their fingernails in the glow, the light reflected on their skin. Then the spices are passed around, everyone breathes in, and the cup is lifted. Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: Hillel won, and the Mishnah still keeps Shammai's words, word for word, beside his. At home, that's the shape of it. One person holds the braid, one holds the spice box, one holds the cup, and everyone looks at their hands in the same light. The week begins together.
screen: `SHAMMAI: ONE LIGHT IN THE FIRE.` · `HILLEL: MANY LIGHTS IN THE FIRE.` · `A BRAIDED CANDLE, MANY WICKS.` · `HANDS UP IN THE SAME LIGHT.` · then, large: `THE WEEK BEGINS TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: If you have a spice nearby, cloves, cinnamon, anything fragrant, hold it close and breathe it in slowly. If not, cup your hands near a lamp or a candle and look at your fingernails in its light. Then name, out loud, one person you'll begin this week with.
screen: `ONE SCENT, OR ONE LIGHT.` · `YOUR HANDS IN THE GLOW.` · `ONE PERSON FOR THE WEEK.`

segments.voice: Havdalah at home: candle, spices and wine, and a flame of many wicks held up with everyone in the house.
Your line: the week begins together, in one light, even on a hard week. Good night, and good week.

howItsDone: On Saturday night, after dark, families say Havdalah at home over a cup of wine or grape juice, a box of fragrant spices and a braided candle with several wicks, sometimes with each person holding one item and everyone looking at their hands in the flame.

Havdalah.meaning: the ceremony that closes Shabbat: candle, spices, wine

Shammai.meaning: an early sage whose school often debated Hillel's

Hillel.meaning: an early sage whose school's rulings usually became law

Mishnah.meaning: the early collection of Jewish law the Talmud discusses

sources.ref: Mishnah Berakhot 8:5 (Shammai: 'who created the light of the fire'; Hillel: 'who creates the lights of the fire')
Mishnah Berakhot 8:6 (no blessing over the light until one benefits from it)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 52b (one light in fire, or many lights)
Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 298 (a torch of several wicks preferred; looking at the fingernails)

notes: Mishnah Berakhot 8:5: Beit Shammai 'shebara me'or ha'esh', Beit Hillel 'borei me'orei ha'esh'; rendered 'who created the light of the fire' / 'who creates the lights of the fire'. Berakhot 52b: both agree 'bara' can mean creates; the dispute is me'or (one light) vs. me'orei (many lights). The voice keeps the Mishnah's wordings; confirm.
Steelman for Shammai ('fire is one thing from one source; name it as one') is the lesson's articulation of 'one light in fire', not a quotation. Confirm it is fair.
Braided candle linked to 'many lights' via the preference for an avukah (torch) in Shulchan Aruch OC 298:2; fingernails custom (298:3). Confirm.
Earlier Havdalah days (y1 day 108 on the spices; y2 days 624-625 on Isaiah 12:2 and Elijah) are not repeated; this day takes the fire debate.
